newsitem.title: USA: NYS Speaker favors LIPA, but energy chair objects.
newsitem.headline: NYS Speaker favors LIPA, but energy chair objects.

text.p: The New York State Assembly Speaker on Tuesday told Governor George Pataki he would go along with Pataki's plan to partly take over the Long Island Lighting Company, but a key Assemblyman objected.

The Republican governor wants the state's Long Island Power Authority (LIPA) to buy assets from LILCO and Brooklyn Union Gas, which are planning to merge. The partial state takeover is designed to lower Long Island's electricity rates, which are among the highest in the nation.

While Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, stated that there was no alternative but to approve the plan, Paul Tonko, D-Montgomery County, head of the Assembly's energy committee recommended that the deal be restructured before approval.

"Without major revision, I recommend that a negative vote be cast by the Assembly representative to the Public Authority Control Board," Tonko told Silver in a July 10 letter that he did not release until Tuesday.
Silver, Pataki and the Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, each hold a seat on the three-member Board, which must approve all tax-exempt bond sales.

The Board next meets on Wednesday, when Silver, whose vote was in doubt after the Assembly held a series of public hearings, now has said he would vote yes if his conditions were accepted. He has said staff members believe it is possible to work out an accord.

The pact aims to cut Long Island's electricity rates, partly by selling $7.3 billion of tax-exempt bonds--the nation's biggest such sale. And LILCO says the deal has to go forward before the Internal Revenue Service publishes new rules to govern how such transactions are treated.
Those rules could impose a $2 billion capital gains tax on LILCO shareholders, which LILCO says would derail the deal.
Asked by Albany reporters why he planned to approve the LIPA bonds on Wednesday, Silver said there was no alternative because the window on the tax-exemption was closing.

"Thereafter, you're left with no alternative but to take the existing plan and try to make it a little better by having the company guarantee the rate savings by advancing the prospects of competition on Long Island by making sure that LILCO invests a substantial portion of the proceeds that they receive in the Long Island region, either in gas or other economic development related activities," he said.

Silver, in a letter to Pataki, said the deal as presently structured would delay developing a competitive marketplace for energy on Long Island. "Neither LIPA nor LILCO have any interest in pursuing a competitive marketplace in Nassau, Suffolk or Queens, and they have made this clear in their testimony."

However, Silver said that trying to acquire LILCO's assets through condemnation could take years of litigation. Getting the Public Service Commission to force the company to compete was not promising, as the Commission's approach to competition has been "exceedingly disappointing," he added.
